data.raw_text:
The NTSB has released its preliminary report on the Dec. 18 plane crash that killed NASCAR great Greg Biffle, his family, and three others.

Based on cockpit recorder audio, multiple cockpit instrument failures occurred shortly after takeoff, with the pilot remarking that his altitude indicator was not working properly and that additional left side flight instruments may also have not been working properly. Around this time, the Garmin navigation system also stopped recording airspeed and heading data.

Based on descriptions, it is presumed that Dennis Dutton was piloting the plane, with his son Jack in the right seat and Greg Biffle seated near the cockpit in the cabin area. There were also discussions of a thrust reverser indicator light(s) for an unspecified engine being inoperative prior to takeoff, but it was said the thrust reverser for the affected engine was working properly. After remarks were made about cockpit instruments not working properly, control of the plane was briefly transferred to Jack Dutton before it is believed control was transferred back to his father.

Following about three minutes of severe degradation in CVR audio quality, the right seat passenger transmitted on the Statesville airport's common traffic advisory frequency that "...we're having some issues here." There was also a query posed by Biffle to the pilot in regards to power to the "alternator" (something the CE-550 is not equipped with), and the pilot "made a comment indicating that was the 'problem'", but there was no specification heard as to what the problem was or what actions were taken to correct it.

In the moments leading up to the crash, the right seat passenger is said to have first visually acquired the runway and given direction to the pilot as to where it was, with the pilot confirming he had acquired visual of the runway at about 10:15:00. Weather conditions reduced visibility to five miles and lowered the ceiling to around 1,200 ft above ground.

Upon final approach to the runway, it was noted that the indicated airspeed of the plane increased from 99 to 107 kts and then back down to ~93 kts during the final five seconds of data. The plane first impacted the easternmost light station of the Medium Intensity Approach Light System leading to runway 28, and then struck a second light station 180 ft ahead from the first identified point of impact before impacting trees 235 ft from the FIPI. A ground impression was noted 350 ft from the FIPI near the airport perimeter fence.

Based on damage patterns, it is believed that both engines appeared to be producing power at impact. 

It was noted that Dennis Dutton's CE-500 type rating required him to have a qualified co-pilot present while operating the plane. Jack Dutton did not have the necessary qualifications to serve as a second-in-command under federal regulations, as it was noted he had 175.3 hours of flight experience and lacked the proper ratings. In Greg Biffle's case, his private pilot certificate had ratings for multi-engine land, instrument airplane and rotorcraft-helicopter.

A probable cause of the crash and any contributing factors will be determined in the final report, which is expected 12-24 months from the accident.
